text: By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion.
On the willows there we hung up our harps,
for there our captors demanded songs of us, our tormentors called for songs of joy: "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"

versions.text: for there our captors demanded songs of us, our tormentors called for joy: "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"
versions.explanation: "Called for joy" is unclear when read aloud — it can sound like they were cheering. The Hebrew ellipsis ("and our tormentors [demanded] mirth") is better carried in English by supplying "songs of joy," which keeps the parallel with the first line and reads smoothly.

text: How can we sing the LORD's song on foreign soil?

If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget how to play.[^1]

[^1]: Hebrew simply reads "may my right hand forget," leaving the object unstated; the context of harp playing (verse 2) is supplied.

versions.text: If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb has no object; "its skill" is an interpretive addition that is not marked. Either mark the addition with a footnote or make the harp connection explicit, since the preceding verse mentions the hung-up harps.

text: Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy.

Remember, LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Tear it down! Tear it down to its foundations!"[^1]

[^1]: "The day of Jerusalem" refers to the day the city fell to its enemies.

versions.text: Remember, LORD, what the Edomites did on the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Tear it down! Tear it down to its foundations!"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew preposition (lit. "remember to/against the sons of Edom") asks God to hold the Edomites accountable; the present rendering weakens this to a mere recollection of their deeds. A brief footnote also helps readers with the idiom "the day of Jerusalem."

text:
Daughter of Babylon, you destroyer,[^1] blessed is the one who repays you for what you did to us,

[^1]: Or "you who are doomed to be destroyed."

versions.text: Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction, blessed is the one who repays you for what you did to us,
versions.explanation: The Hebrew participle is ambiguous (either "the devastated one" or, in an active sense reflected in early tradition, "the devastator"). Since the second half of the verse describes Babylon's deeds against Israel, the active sense fits the flow, and a footnote preserves the alternative.

text: blessed is the one who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rock.
